summary: This document is one of a set describing the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP), a successor to the old WHOIS protocol. It describes how RDAP is carried over the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP). RDAP has an internet-standard status.

plainLanguage.summary: RDAP provides access to domain-name and Internet-number registration data. RFC 7480 explains how RDAP clients and servers exchange requests and responses using HTTP.

subtitle: The HTTP request and response rules used by the Registration Data Access Protocol.

tldr.problem: The older WHOIS protocol does not meet modern registration-data needs, including redirection to authoritative sources and support for internationalized and localized data.
tldr.mechanism: An RDAP client sends an HTTP GET or HEAD request and identifies its desired JSON response format. Servers return data, a redirect, a not-found response, or an error according to the query result and policy.
tldr.outcome: The HTTP profile gives clients a common way to query registration-data services. RFC 7480 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated in the unit metadata.

today: RFC 7480 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why RDAP Uses HTTP
sections.content:
RFC 7480 is one of a set of documents that describe the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP), a successor to WHOIS. It defines how RDAP uses standard HTTP mechanisms to access Internet resource registration data, including domain names and Internet number resources.

The profile aims to give different directory services common behavior so one client can query them consistently. It keeps the client simple and places more of the service-specific complexity on the server. The document does not redefine HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: RDAP uses HTTP so clients can query different registration-data services in a consistent way. This RFC defines how the client and server use HTTP for those exchanges.

sections.title: One Query Path and Common HTTP Tools
sections.content:
The RFC's design goal is for each query to follow one path to an answer. A server can return the answer, indicate that there is no answer, or redirect the client. Clients are not expected to try multiple query paths at once.

RDAP uses HTTP features such as caching, authorization, compression, and redirection according to local policy. Query formats and JSON response contents are specified in separate RDAP documents; RFC 7480 focuses on transporting them over HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: A client makes one request and follows the response it receives. Other RDAP specifications define the query and response data formats.

sections.title: Sending an RDAP Query
sections.content:
Clients use GET to retrieve a response body and may use HEAD to determine whether data exists. Clients and servers must support HTTPS. To request an RDAP response, the client sends an Accept field with an RDAP-specific JSON media type, the generic JSON media type, or both.

A server returns the RDAP-specific JSON media type in Content-Type. The RFC does not define the response to a request with a different or absent Accept field. Servers must ignore unknown query parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The client uses a normal HTTP request and states that it wants RDAP data in JSON. The server must ignore query parameters it does not recognize.

sections.title: Answers, Errors, and Redirects
sections.content:
A server with data returns a 200 OK response. If the data is elsewhere, it returns a redirection response and a complete HTTP(S) URL in Location; the client follows that URL without transforming it. A 404 Not Found response means the result set is empty.

A server can use an HTTP 4xx response when policy prevents it from giving available information, and 400 Bad Request when it cannot interpret the query as RDAP. A rate-limited server returns 429 Too Many Requests; clients should reduce their query rate and honor Retry-After when present.
sections.plainLanguage: The response tells the client whether the data is available, elsewhere, absent, or unavailable under the server's policy. A rate-limit response asks the client to slow down.

sections.title: Extensions and Internationalized Data
sections.content:
The RFC creates a registry for extension identifiers used as prefixes in JSON names and URL path segments. Identifiers should use letters, digits, and underscores, with restrictions on their first characters. New identifiers require a permanent reference that describes their meaning sufficiently for independent implementations to interoperate.

Clients may use Internationalized Resource Identifiers internally, but must convert them to Uniform Resource Identifiers when communicating with servers. Servers must use URIs in responses. When a server knows the language of returned data, it should label that data with a language identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: RDAP extensions use registered names so different services can avoid naming conflicts. Clients and servers use standard web addresses in their messages, even if clients keep internationalized forms internally.

sections.title: Security and Status Today
sections.content:
RFC 7480 requires RDAP clients and servers to support HTTPS, while referring to RFC 7481 for additional RDAP security considerations. For browser clients, servers are recommended to send the CORS Access-Control-Allow-Origin field. The RFC does not recommend enabling cross-origin credentials with cookies.

RFC 7480 is an Internet Standard. Unit metadata does not list a later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.
sections.plainLanguage: RDAP clients and servers must support HTTPS. The RFC also describes a browser setting that permits access to public RDAP data from another site.
